prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Other weddings are so shrewd on the sofa, short and baffled, bassett-legged. All things knuckled, I have no winter left, in my sore rememory, to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slides the way wiry dark hairs do, down a swimming pool drain. So I am drained. Sincerely. I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem up from the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink in the sun, I will crawl towards the heavy drawing and design the curtains in the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking, because today’s perfect weather is a later life’s smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier, I have no garden and couldn’t be happier. Please, don’t lose me here. I am sorry my clutch is all tendon and no discipline: the heart is a severed kind of muscle and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another room. In another’s.

Here are two refined options depending on the exact tone you wish to achieve:

### Option 1: High Literary & Lyrical (Recommended)
*This version smooths out the rhythm and elevates the vocabulary while fully preserving the poetic, avant-garde voice of the original.*

> Other weddings sit awkwardly upon the sofa—stubby, baffled, and short-limbed. With everything worn down to the knuckle, I have no winter left in my aching memory to melt down into drinking water; I am entirely diminished. Your wedding slips away the way dark, wiry hairs do down a swimming pool drain, leaving me utterly drained. Sincerely. I wish you every weathered bird on this pilgrimage to lift your hem above the dust—and dust is plural, an infinity of dust. 
>
> I shall sink beneath the sun; I will crawl toward the heavy drafts and design the curtains for the room where I never marry you. For this is a descent, and today’s flawless weather will become the grime of a later life. This tarnished future unplans love. I continuously undo the same envisioned Sunday. Leg and blossom, breeze and terrier—I possess no garden, and I could not be happier. 
>
> Please, do not lose me here. I am sorry my grasp is all desperate tendon and no restraint; the heart is a severed sort of muscle, solitary and alone. I can hear yours beating in your room. I hear mine in a different room altogether—in someone else’s.

---

### Option 2: Elegant & Refined Prose
*This version structures the thoughts into a slightly more fluid, formal narrative while retaining every original detail.*

> In contrast, other weddings appear crude upon the sofa—short, bewildered, and ungainly. Reduced to the bare knuckle, my sore memory holds no remaining winter to melt for drinking water; I am completely shrunk down. Your wedding slides away like dark, wiry strands down a pool drain, leaving me drained of everything. Truly, I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem above the dust—an infinite, plural dust. 
>
> I will sink into the sun; I will crawl toward the heavy draft work to design curtains for the room of never marrying you. It is a slow sinking, knowing that today’s perfect weather will become the residue of a later life. This soiled future systematically unplans love, just as I keep unplanning the exact same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier—I have no garden, and I could not be happier. 
>
> Please, do not lose sight of me here. Forgive me that my hold is pure tendon without discipline; the heart, after all, is a severed muscle, existing in isolation. I can hear yours from your room. I hear mine in another room entirely—belonging to another.

---

### Key Enhancements Made:
*   **Rhythm & Cadence:** Sentence structures were re-balanced so the prose flows seamlessly when read aloud.
*   **Precision:** Words like *rememory* were translated into *aching memory*, and *clutch* into *grasp/hold*, clarifying the emotional weight without losing the imagery.
*   **Punctuation:** Em-dashes and semicolons were introduced to connect fragmented thoughts into cohesive, dramatic beats.

Most other nuptial unions appear crafty yet squat, bewildered, and short-limbed as they rest upon a couch. With every joint clenched tight, my aching memory holds no leftover frost to thaw into drinking water; everything has shriveled. Meanwhile, your marriage slips away like coarse, dark strands washing down a pool's drain outlet. Because of this, I am completely emptied out—truly. 

I hope that every raw, weathered bird along this journey will lift the edge of your dress above the dirt. That grime is vast and boundless. I am bound to collapse under the bright sunlight, dragging myself to sketch the window drapes inside a chamber where we never wed. It is a total descent, for today's ideal climate will turn into the soot of a future age. This tarnished tomorrow undoes affection; I repeatedly dismantle the blueprint of that exact Sunday. 

Amidst limbs, blooms, gusts of air, and small dogs, I possess no yard and am thoroughly glad for it. I beg you not to abandon me at this point. Forgive me that my grip is sheer sinew lacking self-control; the heart is merely a detached organ, standing by itself. I can detect your pulse beating in your space, while mine thumps in a separate room entirely—one that belongs to another person.

Here is a fully expanded, cohesive text based on your bullet points, written in the style of a poignant letter or dramatic monologue:

***

To see the reality of your wedding day finally unfold has left me entirely hollowed out. Whatever resolve I pretended to hold has completely evaporated, leaving me drained and depleted in a way I have never known. The sheer finality of it all has taken root, forcing me to confront the devastating truth that you belong to someone else now. 

And yet, even beneath the crushing weight of my own sorrow, I offer you my blessing. It is a quiet, somber wish for your joy on this new journey you are beginning—a blessing spoken through a grief so overwhelming that it threatens to consume me entirely. I genuinely hope you find the happiness you sought, even as my own world collapses in the wake of yours.

I am forced now to resign myself to the cold reality of a solitary future. The life we built together, woven over years of quiet intimacy and shared dreams, feels permanently undone. Every connection we forged has been untangled, leaving me to navigate a quiet, empty existence defined by the profound absence of what we used to be. 

Forgive me, for I no longer possess the strength to conceal my composure. In this moment of raw vulnerability, dignity gives way to sheer desperation, and I am reduced to a pleading voice. Please, I beg you, do not let me fade into the background of your past. Do not leave me behind in the shadow of your new life, entirely forgotten as if our history were nothing more than a momentary distraction.

I have come to realize that the human heart is an inherently isolated organ, doomed to beat alone within its own quiet cage. Looking at you now, the emotional and physical distance that stretches between us feels vast, absolute, and impassable. You have moved into a world I cannot enter, leaving me alone on the far side of a divide that can never be crossed again.
outputs.L4:
The news did not arrive like a sound, but like a physical puncture—a cold, sharp insertion directly beneath the ribs. You had stood at an altar built of someone else’s promises, exchanging vows that were never meant for me, placing your tomorrows into the hands of a stranger. In that single moment, the reality we had shared shattered, and the long, agonizing process of dismantling what should have been began.

What followed was the grotesque, surreal labor of unmaking an entire existence. Grief became a physical entity, heavy and suffocating. In the dark theatre of my mind, I was forced to walk through the quiet, unbuilt rooms of our future and tear them down, wall by wall. I had to un-key the front door of the house we would never buy. I had to un-plant the garden that was supposed to bloom in our twilight years. One by one, I gathered the names we had quietly picked for children who would now never be born, and swallowed them back down into the dark, letting them dissolve into quiet dust. I scraped the sound of your imagined laughter off the walls of my mind, untied our hands from phantom anniversaries, and systematically burned the unlived years like dry linen.

As the days bled together, the pain morphed into something visceral and strange. The world outside lost its anchor; colors bled out into bruised shades of grey, and the air turned thick as water. I watched my own body from a distance—a hollow shell filled with wet ash and silent alarms. In dreams, your wedding ring was not gold, but a heavy iron collar sinking into a dark sea, dragging the memory of us down with it. I tried to reach for the ghost of your touch, but my fingers passed through cold, empty air, leaving behind only the metallic sting of phantom loss. The sheer magnitude of the sorrow distorted everything, turning memory into a minefield and hope into a cruel, impossible language I could no longer speak.

Eventually, the screaming inside my chest did not stop so much as it simply ran out of fuel. The acute agony burned through every soft, vulnerable part of me, leaving behind a stark, desolate calm. A heavy numbness settled into my bones—a profound, icy detachment that pushed the rest of the world to an infinite distance. 

Now, I look out at the light through thick glass, entirely untouched by it. The unplanning is complete, but the cost was absolute. Heartbreak of this severity does not merely break a spirit; it fundamentally alters the architecture of a soul, severing the delicate threads that connect one person to the rest of humanity. The fire has consumed itself, leaving no warmth, no anger, and no path back. Drained of color and emptied of expectation, I remain suspended in this quiet, unyielding void—a spectator to a world I no longer belong to, where the heart is left to exist entirely, irrevocably alone.
outputs.L5:
When I returned to the old house at the end of the lane, the world seemed strangely reduced. The grand staircase that once felt like a mountain now took only a few strides to climb, and the endless backyard had **shrunk** into a humble patch of lawn bordered by a faded wooden fence. 

It is a curious trick of time and perspective. As children, **all** the possibilities of the universe seem vast and uncontained, stretching far beyond the visible horizon. We believe every room holds a secret, every summer lasts forever, and our ambitions are boundless. 

Yet, standing on that quiet porch years later, I realized that the physical space hadn't changed at all—only my frame of reference had expanded. I looked down the quiet street, watching a car disappear around the bend, and thought of the **other** lives I might have led had I chosen a different path. We often spend our youth chasing the vastness of the world, only to discover later that meaning isn't found in infinite scale, but in the quiet, focused places we choose to call home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about the complex, visceral grief of watching an ex-lover marry someone else. Use strange domestic imagery and themes of isolation.
counterfactuals.output:
Today, you are threading a golden circle onto a finger that isn’t mine, and in my kitchen, the linoleum peels back like wet skin. I sit at the laminate table and swallow a spoonful of the salt you left behind, waiting for it to curdle the milk in my stomach. Miles away, beneath a canopy of trembling orchids, you kiss her mouth; here, my ceiling fan spins backward, unthreading the room until I am inhaling heavy, suffocating velvet. 

I hear your *I do* humming up through the garbage disposal, rattling the rusted blades. I try to fold the bedsheets, but they are stiff with old grease; every time I tuck a corner under the mattress, a rib in my torso snaps like dry pine. She wears white, they say. I wear the pilot light that died three Tuesdays ago, dusting my shoulders in soot. On the dining room wall, the wallpaper begins to sweat small, translucent ants that carry away the crumbs of our former names. 

Now they are cutting the cake. A silver blade glides through four tiers of buttercream, but in my living room, the upholstery softens, swallowing my knees, my hips, my wrists, until I am nothing but a throat resting on the sofa cushions. I open my mouth to call out, to object, but out comes a cloud of mothballs and lavender dust. You fill stacked towers of crystal with champagne. I drink tap water that tastes like the copper under your tongue—the copper I am no longer licensed to remember.

The music starts. You lead her into the first dance, your palm flat against the small of her back. I press my ear to the cold porcelain of the bathtub and listen to the plumbing sing your new surname. The house shrinks around me, wall by wall, ceiling to floor, until there is only this dark pantry, an empty jar of peach jam, and me—kneeling on the floorboards, chewing slowly on the hem of a veil I was never meant to wear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of experimental flash fiction in the voice of someone writing an unsent letter to their former partner on their wedding day. Make it poetic, tragic, and filled with striking, strange metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
**To the Groom / To the Scaffolding of a Man I Used to Know**

**[11:04 AM]**
The sun today is a yellow tooth rotting in the mouth of the sky. 

Somewhere six miles south, a tailor is tugging an iron thread through your lapel, pinning you into your new symmetry. You are putting on your shoes. I know the way you pull the laces—a double knot like a small, panicked fist. 

I am sitting on my kitchen floor, trying to remember the sound of your collarbone breaking against the summer.

***

**[12:30 PM]**
Is the aisle long enough for you to walk off the marrow I gave you?

The church bells are heavy copper fruit dropping from a dead tree. I can feel their vibrations in my molars. You are standing at the front now, under the stained glass that paints your suit the color of bruised plums. A man in white robes, sewn from bleached bedsheets, is rewiring your nervous system. He takes your left atrium and solders it to her wrist. 

I am left here with the spare spool of wire, sparking against the wet linoleum.

***

**[1:15 PM]**
You are saying the vow. 

The word *husband* is a lead sinker dropped into a well full of warm milk. It goes down thick and silent. 

When you kiss her, do you taste the copper in my throat? Does a phantom limb reach out from your hip pocket to look for the keys we threw into the quarry five years ago? She is beautiful, I’m sure. A porcelain vessel built to hold the water you kept dropping from your palms. But under that stiff white lace, does she know your ribs are made from the handrails of my old apartment? Every time you take a deep breath, you are just climbing the stairs to a room where I am still waiting.

***

**[2:45 PM]**
They are cutting the cake now. Three tiers of sweetened chalk and soft plaster. 

I hope it tastes like wet drywall. I hope the champagne un-knits your blood. 

I am not burning this letter. Fire is too clean for what we built. Instead, I am folding the paper into the shape of an artificial lung. I am breath-stuffed and heavy. I will bury it under the sink, behind the bleach, where the dark stays wet.

***

**[4:00 PM]**
Congratulations. You have successfully un-invented us. 

I am going to close my eyes now and let the afternoon perform its slow, blind autopsy. Do not look for my face in the blurred edge of your wedding photos. I am the shadow the camera refused to catch—the extra shadow you’ll have to drag behind you for the rest of your life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a prose poem about heartbreak styled after modern poets like Richard Siken or Ocean Vuong? Focus on the physical sensation of emotional exhaustion and missing out on a future together.
counterfactuals.output: There is a sandbag sewn into the soft velvet beneath my sternum, and every step I take today is a renegotiation with gravity. I am so tired my teeth feel like borrowed chalk. Listen: this is how a body surrenders—not with a white flag, but like a house losing its drywall to a slow, silent flood until only the timber remains, shivering in the dark. We were supposed to buy the cheap couch. We were supposed to grow old until our faces looked like crumpled receipts at the bottom of a winter coat, until our names were just a shorthand we used to find each other in a crowded room. Now, the future is an empty museum where I am the only patron, walking past pedestals holding nothing at all. I sit on the edge of the mattress and feel the weight of thirty unspent years sitting beside me, heavy as wet wool, pressing their cold foreheads against my ribs. Tell me how to un-learn the architecture of your collarbone. Tell me how to stop reaching across the bed for a ghost that doesn't even have the courtesy to haunt me properly. In the kitchen, the sunlight comes through the blinds like the fluorescent lighting of an operating room, sterile and relentless, illuminating the quiet space where we were supposed to drink coffee at sixty. I carry the dead years in my throat. I swallow them down, through the floorboards, through the floorboards, into the dark earth beneath the foundation. Look at us: two boys who built a temple out of breath and then forgot how to breathe. I am so exhausted I could sleep inside a fist. I am still here, holding the blueprints to a city that burned before we ever laid the first stone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic monologue about an ex getting married.
counterfactuals.output:
*(The speaker sits at a kitchen table late at night. The only light comes from a phone screen resting face-down on the wood. They are staring into an empty mug, tracing the rim with a index finger.)*

I saw the photos today. 

Someone posted them online. I knew it was coming—I’ve known the date for months, drawn like a quiet little red circle in the back of my mind. But seeing it… that’s different. 

You looked… incredible. Truly. You had that specific, crooked smile—the one you only make when you’re trying not to cry. You wore the navy suit. The one we bought together three years ago for your sister’s graduation. You always said it made your shoulders look broad. I guess you were right. 

It’s a strange thing, isn't it? Watching someone build the exact house you spent years drafting the blueprints for. 

I looked at her. She was beautiful. Really, she was. And the way you held her hand… you did that thing with your thumb, pressing it gently into the back of her knuckles. You used to do that to me whenever I was nervous in a crowd. I wondered, looking at that picture, if it’s just a reflex for you now. Or if you even remember where you learned to do it.

It doesn't make me angry. I thought it would, but it doesn't. It just feels… hollow. Like coming back to the town you grew up in and finding out they tore down your childhood home to build a parking lot. You can’t really be mad at the asphalt, can you? Progress is just progress. Life just… moves forward. 

We spent four years talking about forever. We picked out baby names on a napkin in a diner at two in the morning. We swore, back when we were young and arrogant enough to believe it, that no matter what happened, we’d always belong to each other in some small way. 

But watching you dip her on the dance floor… I realized that forever isn't a promise. It’s just an expiration date we couldn't see. 

I’m happy for you. God, I really am. You deserve the world, and it looks like she gives it to you. But a part of me—just a tiny, foolish part—wonders if, right before you said "I do," when the music swelled and everyone stood up… if you took a breath, and for a fraction of a second, remembered my name. 

*(They pause, taking a slow, heavy breath. They reach out and gently turn the phone screen off, plunging the table into darkness.)*

Probably not. And… I suppose that’s the way it’s supposed to be. 

Goodnight. And congratulations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a short, poetic passage about an unwanted wedding day. Incorporate sensory details related to dust, rooms, muscles, and the feeling of unravelling a planned future.
counterfactuals.output:
The waiting room smells of dried lilies and ancient plaster, illuminated by a slanting shaft of sunlight where static dust dances, slow and indifferent. Beneath the suffocating weight of white silk, my muscles coil into tight, silent knots—my jaw clenched against a breath I cannot fully release, my shoulders bracing as if for a collision. Each chamber of this sanctuary feels smaller than the last, trapping me in a procession of rooms I never wished to walk through. 

As the organ’s first heavy chord strikes the air, the pristine tapestry of my planned future begins to fray. It is a quiet, visceral unravelling: thread by thread, the neat blueprint of a life drawn by others pulls apart, unspooling onto the cold floor like loose lace, leaving me to step into the dark space of a tomorrow I never asked to inherit.
